newsitem.title: USA: Tests finished on nerve gas destroyer.
newsitem.headline: Tests finished on nerve gas destroyer.

text.p: A company developing a way to destroy nerve gas and other deadly substances without incineration has successfully destroyed the explosive components of a nerve gas rocket, it said Thursday.

The results mean the chemical process developed by Teledyne-Commodore LLC has passed the last of four tests critical to competing for an Army programme for alternative means of destroying stockpiles of assembled chemical weapons, the company said.

The process -- known as solvated electron technology, or SET -- destroyed the explosive component and propellant of an M55 nerve gas rocket at an Army-certified laboratory, Huntsville, Ala.-based Teledyne-Commodore said.

SET has already been shown to destroy all six stockpiled war gases, including mustard gas and Sarin and VX nerve gases and decontaminate the weapons' metal components and packing material, the company said.

Teledyne-Commodore is a joint venture of Pittsburgh-based Allegheny Teledyne Inc. and New York-based Commodore Applied Technologies Inc. Commodore's stock gained $2 to $7.625 on the American Stock Exchange, and Allegheny added 50 cents to $23.75 on the New York Stock Exchange.

"This technology sounds promising," said Suzanne Fournier, a spokeswoman for the Army Chemical and Biological Defence Command at Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland. "It will be assessed with a number of other technologies that are brought forth."

She said others in the private sector and academia are expected to compete for the programme, aimed at finding a way to destroy assembled chemical weapons like rockets and artillery projectiles without using incineration.

Under the international Chemical Weapons Convention signed by President Clinton in 1993, the Defence Department must destroy U.S. stockpiles of poison gas and other chemical weapons by the year 2007. Other nations must do likewise.

"The demilitarization of these materials using methods other than incineration has been one of the most difficult tasks in the Department of Defence Chemical Weapons Programme," said Teledyne-Commodore President Gerald Watson.

"We consider this a major breakthrough in the search for alternative non-thermal technologies capable of destroying explosive materials in chemical weapons," said Watson, a retired major general who was a leading chemical officer with the Army.

Incineration as a way of disposing of chemical weapons and other toxic susbstances has stirred controversy because of fears of exhaust gases from incineration despite the presence of government-required air pollution control devices.
SET, which uses commonly available chemicals, can also be used to destroy polychlorinated biphenyls, or PCBs, dioxin and pesticides, Commodore said.

The process works by placing the toxic substance to be destroyed in a tank with anhydrous, or water-free, ammonia. Metallic sodium is then added to the mix and dissolved in the ammonia. When the resulting solution turns a vivid blue, it indicates the toxic substance is being neutralised. The resulting mix -- now non-toxic -- is removed and any by-products needing further processing can receive further treatment.
The ammonia solution used in the process can be recycled and reused, the company said.

Chemical agents have been stored for over 40 years at eight U.S. Army bases in the continental United States, including the Aberdeen Proving Ground, the Anniston Army Depot in Alabama and Pine Bluff Arsenal in Arkansas. Chemical munitions are also stored on Johnston Island in the Pacific. These munitions were removed from forward deployed depots in Europe and the Far East.
